GLM: FULL-PR adversarial review: bolt-v2 #1218 (surface: run_manifest.rs, runner.rs)
Per-guarantee verdict
#1 Production parity — HOLDS. The maker is constructed via the shared production_strategy_registry().register_strategy(key, raw, &ctx, trader) → BinaryOracleMakerBuilder::register → BinaryOracleMaker::new(parse_config(raw)?, ctx) (runner.rs:681-688, src/strategies/binary_oracle_maker/mod.rs impl StrategyBuilder). This is the same trait path the live archetype uses (archetype.rs:798-805). No forked parse, no forked registration. The one context difference — empty RV runtime in backtest vs the node's in live — is behaviorally inert (see #3).
#2 Allowlist discipline — HOLDS. Unknown keys hit the other => bail!("… not a registered compiled Rust strategy") gate at runner.rs:918, pinned by unknown_manifest_strategy_still_fails_allowlist (runner.rs:2826). The maker arm rejects config_overlay, parses+range-checks fee_bps, parses order_execution_mode, parses config_toml, and runs registry.validate on it before any build (run_manifest.rs:1169-1230, runner.rs:844-863).
#3 Fail-closed on missing RV — HOLDS (vacuously, and that's the strongest form). The maker is structurally incapable of consuming RV: BinaryOracleMakerConfig has no RV field and is deny_unknown_fields (config.rs:35-88), and the maker module never dereferences any RV accessor — verified zero reads across mod.rs/runtime.rs/binding.rs/mu.rs; the sole reference is archetype.rs:795 threading the runtime into the context, never read back. So "a maker config that REQUIRES RV" is impossible and the empty runtime is inert. There is no silent-quote-on-missing-RV path because the maker doesn't quote on RV at all (it quotes on μ + reference fair value, and the autonomous loop doesn't even call run_quote_cycle yet).
#4 Smoke is real — PARTIAL (one LOW finding, below). Fixture itself is sound (see attack area C); the gap is assertion depth.
#5 No literals in shared code — HOLDS. Shared code uses key, manifest.venue.nt_venue.as_str(), and binary_oracle_maker::KEY (sourced from the live module's KEY const, run_manifest.rs:57). All venue/instrument literals (MAKER_SMOKE_*, "POLYMARKET") are confined to the #[cfg(test)] block.
Findings
LOW — runner.rs:2808-2834 binary_oracle_maker_manifest_runs_through_backtest_node asserts engine plumbing, not maker behavior.
The four asserts are: run_config_id identity, iterations == 2, config_override_report.is_none(), run_guard_report.is_some(). iterations counts engine data points delivered (runner.rs:2025, "once per data point delivered to the engine loop"), not strategy callbacks — so a maker whose on_start market-resolution or on_trade μ-feed silently regressed to a no-op would still satisfy iterations == 2. run_guard_report carries armed/traded/did_not_arm_reason (runner.rs:146-195) but only .is_some() is checked (and it is Some by construction at runner.rs:1169-1172). The smoke proves registration didn't panic and the engine consumed the catalog; it does not prove the declared market resolved, that μ observed the ticks, or that any maker code path engaged. Mitigation: the maker doesn't quote autonomously yet (run_quote_cycle is differential-test-only per its doc comment), so orders/evidence aren't available to assert, and μ-feeding has unit coverage (mod.rs::on_trade_feeds_the_mu_buffer). Still, by the review's own bar ("orders, evidence, contract fields, not merely 'it ran without error'"), this smoke is below the line — a market-resolution/μ-observation assertion (or a log-capture of refresh_active_markets misses) would close it.
Attack-area resolution
A. Invalid→MissingField mapping (run_manifest.rs:1199-1209, 1216): NO divergence. The taker arm maps bad execution-mode / negative fee / unparseable config to MissingField identically (run_manifest.rs:1132-1142, 1150, 1163). The repo does have ManifestError::UnsupportedEnum (used by the mechanical-probe arm, run_manifest.rs:1260/1274/1288/1298) but the binary-oracle family uniformly uses MissingField. This is a consistent convention, not a maker/taker divergence. (Pre-existing mislabel — an operator with a negative fee gets a "MissingField" message — but neither introduced nor worsened by this PR; not a finding against #1218.)
B. registry.validate (manifest time) vs register_strategy (build time): asymmetry exists, but pre-existing and taker-consistent. validate_config (config.rs:140-215) checks envelope strings + markets_config_digest presence + oms_type parses + order_id_tag delimiter-free; it does not check μ-knob presence/type. parse_config (serde, deny_unknown_fields, all fields required) does. So a config missing trade_flow_window_secs etc. passes registry.validate/manifest.validate but fails at register_strategy. Direction: passes-validate, fails-register. The taker has the same shape, so this is not maker-introduced. Concrete impact on this PR's paths: in run_nt_backtest_node (the smoke entry, runner.rs:1099) manifest.validate() is not called at all — add_manifest_strategy → register_manifest_binary_oracle_strategy → register_strategy → parse_config is the authoritative gate, and it catches everything fail-closed. So there is no silent-pass path; only the error category/wording differs. No action required for this PR.
C. Smoke fixture vacuousness: fixture is SOUND, not vacuous. Traced the matching: instruments SAMPLE-EVENT-{YES,NO}.POLYMARKET carry info metadata (market_slug="will-sample-event-resolve-yes", condition_id="condition-sample-event", market_id="sample-event-yes-no", question_id="question-sample-event") and outcomes "Yes"/"No" (runner.rs:2556-2587); the declared static market (cadence_slug_token/static_condition_id/static_yes_outcome/static_no_outcome) matches via select_static_market_from_instruments (static_binary_event.rs:540-599 — slug match → outcome Up/Down → common market_id/condition/slug/question → expiry gate). Activation (TS-1s) and expiry (TS+60s) bracket the trades (TS, TS+1ms), and the engine clock at on_start (epoch or first-tick) is ≪ expiry, so expiration_milliseconds <= now_milliseconds is false and the market resolves. Price/qty (0.500/1.00, 3/2 precision) are valid for the 0.001–0.999 price bounds. The fixture engages the maker's real resolution path; the weakness is the assertions (finding LOW above), not the fixture.
Deferred follow-ups (a)/(b) — not reported, per scope. Confirmed the taker inlines its own context build (runner.rs:756-820) while the maker uses the new shared register_manifest_binary_oracle_strategy helper — the documented dual-path deferral; maker RV plumbing likewise deferred.
Bottom line
No HIGH/MEDIUM/CRITICAL. The four substantive guarantees (#1, #2, #3, #5) hold with the reasoning above. One LOW finding on the smoke's assertion depth (#4). Two pre-existing, taker-consistent asymmetries (invalid→MissingField; validate-vs-register coverage) are noted as informational, not actioned — this PR inherits them faithfully without divergence.

**Panel packet for PR #1226 (Brief 3, loss-halt recovery command):**

```
Review request: bolt-v2 PR #1226 — FULL-PR adversarial review. LIVE KILL-SWITCH SAFETY CODE.

Repo: https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2
PR:   https://github.com/seungpyoson/bolt-v2/pull/1226
Base: merge-base with origin/main (branch cut post-#1185, >= f57df1916)
Head:        78dfd70fb392626d677b16d084885de089395f8e
Surface: src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs (durable-store schema + append API),
NEW src/bolt_v3_loss_governor_manual_recovery_ops.rs (452 lines, the command),
src/main.rs (ops subcommand wiring), src/lib.rs, tests ×3, runtime-literal audit re-anchor.

Context: operators previously had NO shipped way to clear a loss-governor halt — the recovery
function existed but nothing reached it. This PR adds `ops loss-governor-manual-recovery`:
offline (node stopped, mirroring InitKillSwitchStore's posture), driving the EXISTING
evaluate_loss_admission + next_loss_governor_manual_recovery_trading_state +
LossGovernorManualRecoveryEvidence validation — no forked state machine — and persisting an
append-only manual-recovery audit history as a NEW additive optional field
(loss_governor_manual_recoveries) in the durable kill-switch store (schema version unbumped,
old stores parse to empty history, field serialized only when non-empty).

Claimed guarantees — try to break each:
1. #1185 conformance (binding rules from the merged Lane 3): non-armed states are never
   downgraded outside the sanctioned loss-governor halt path; successful recovery is
   write-through durable Armed + preserved loss snapshot + audit; recovery-write failure
   attempts FailedManualIntervention persistence, both-failed is its own loud error; nothing
   silently succeeds.
2. Evidence contract: no path constructs or applies a recovery without
   LossGovernorManualRecoveryEvidence::new validation (operator id, evidence sha256,
   observed-at) plus the UnauthorizedOperator check — verify where the authorized-operator set
   comes from and whether it can be empty/bypassed.
3. Fail-closed store handling: missing store, corrupt store, oversized store, wrong schema
   version, non-loss-governor states, unsupported states — each a distinct loud error, no
   auto-create, history never deleted.
4. Schema compatibility BOTH directions: old store + new binary (must parse, empty history);
   new store + old binary (what exactly happens — fail-closed halt is acceptable, silent
   misread is not).
5. The audit-history preservation path: routine write_state_with_loss_snapshot re-reads and
   carries history forward; on a failed read it now LOGS log::error (path + error + explicit
   empty-history statement) and proceeds — verify the regression test genuinely exercises the
   Err branch and that no OTHER writer path can still drop history silently
   (write_loss_governor_manual_recovery, bootstrap paths).

Specific attack areas:
- Concurrency posture: the command assumes the node is STOPPED (documented, mirroring
  InitKillSwitchStore). Probe the consequence of violating it: node running + offline recovery
  → the node's next state write re-reads history (preserved?) but can it overwrite/negate the
  recovery Armed state, or double-apply? Is last-writer-wins here safe, and is the posture
  loudly documented for operators?
- Unbounded history growth: recoveries append forever into a store guarded by
  ensure_state_bytes_within_limit — after enough entries, does routine state persistence start
  FAILING (fail-closed brick of halt recording)? What's the limit vs per-record size math?
- Evidence file handling: path/size limits on the evidence file
  (manual_recovery_evidence_max_path_bytes existed in the runtime path) — mirrored here?
- Degraded-state invariants: --help from any directory with no config; nonexistent state path
  exits non-zero with a clear message (tests claimed — verify).
- The now_ns source for the offline command (clock trust for evaluate_loss_admission's
  staleness math).

Evidence on file (verify, don't trust): red proof run 28710073223 at pre-impl commit 7110259e9
(missing-symbol failures quoted); final full CI 28713654494 green at exactly 78dfd70fb; a
superseded run 28713098359 that caught the first regression test not exercising the Err branch
(then fixed); deviations declared (draft-toggle ×2 for dispatch, one probe dead on infra).

Report findings as: severity / file + symbol anchor / concrete failure scenario.
"Looks fine" only per-guarantee, with reasoning stated.

PR 1226

Claude:
PR #1226 — Loss-governor manual recovery ops command — Adversarial FULL-PR review

Range (pinned): base f57df191682ef6384dc9b3b6eb98098189947456 (= merge-base, ✓ ≥ f57df1916) → head 78dfd70fb392626d677b16d084885de089395f8e. 8 files, +1147/-4.

Bottom line: The core safety guarantees hold. The gating is sound — non-loss-governor and non-halt states are correctly refused, evidence is validated before anything is written, the store is fail-closed on every corruption class, and the append writer preserves history. I found no HIGH/critical correctness defect that makes the happy path unsafe. I did find one MEDIUM architectural coupling and three lower items, all in the "harden before this sees heavy production use" bucket, plus one framing note operators must understand. I'm not declaring merge-readiness — reporting state + evidence below.

Evidence chain — personally verified (not trusted):
- Green CI 28713654494 = success at exactly head 78dfd70fb… (workflow CI [dispatch:full]). ✓
- Red proof 28710073223 at pre-impl 7110259e9 = failure with error[E0432]: unresolved import …loss_governor_manual_recovery_ops + error[E0609]: no field loss_governor_manual_recoveries — genuine missing-symbol/differential failure. ✓
- Superseded 28713098359 = failure; the captured commit diff shows the first regression test used fs::write(path, b"{not-json") (corrupt-in-place) and was rewritten to fs::set_permissions(0o200) (unreadable). This independently confirms the corrupt path does not log. ✓

---
Findings (severity-ranked)

1. MEDIUM — Unbounded audit history shares the 64 KB byte-capped safety-state file; growth can brick halt recording

src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs — write_loss_governor_manual_recovery / ensure_state_bytes_within_limit; consequence at src/bolt_v3_basket_execut file also carries the loss-protection snapshot with position-PnL maps. After roughly 150–240 recoveries the serialized state exceeds 64 KB.

Failure scenario: once near the cap, the node's routine halt-recording path — write_state(&halting/&halted/&failed) at bolt_v3_basket_execution.rs:880-913, which routes through write_state_with_loss_snapshot → re-reads and re-appends the whole history → StateTooLarge. The &failed (FailedManualIntervention) fallback is let _ = write_state(&failed) (line 890/913) — it also re-appends the oversized history, also fails, and the error is discarded. Net: a full store can silently prevent the node from durably recording a new halt; on restart the store shows the last-written (possibly Armed) state. Probability is low (manual recoveries are rare operator events), but this couples an audit feature to safety-state persistence reliability — backwards for kill-switch code, and it's a class problem (unbounded data in a bounded safety file), not an instance. Recommend separating the audit trail from the byte-capped state file, o

src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs:137-151 — existing_loss_governor_manual_recoveries.

The fix logs log::error! only on the Err arm. But load_recovery_record returns Ok(FailClosed{…, manual_recoveries: vec![]}) for corrupt (:254) and oversized (:242) stores — those take the Ok branch, return empty, and the subsequent write_state_with_loss_snapshot overwrites with empty history with no log. This is precisely the branch the PR's own first regression test accidentally hit (corrupt-in-place → no log fired → assertion failed → rewritten to a permission error). Corrupt is low-impact (data already unparseable), butcode and operator docs

src/bolt_v3_loss_governor_manual_recovery_ops.rs — recover_loss_governor_manual_halt (no doc comment; grep found no "node stopped/offline" note anywhere except the PR description).

The command writes via write_private_atomic_file (unconditional rename) — unlike InitKillSwitchStore's write_private_new_file (O_EXCL), it has no detection of a running node. If run while the node is live, it's last-writer-wins: the node's next write_state reverts Armed→Halted (safe direction, but the operator saw a false "completed": true), or thmirroring InitKillSwitchStore" claim isn't reflected anywhere an operator would see it. Add a doc comment + runbook line stating the node must be stopped.

4. LOW — Coverage gaps on safety-relevant paths

tests/bolt_v3_loss_governor_manual_recovery_ops.rs.

Tested: happy path + audit persistence, invalid-evidence refusal, non-loss-governor no-downgrade, missing-store fail-closed. Untested: UnauthorizedOperator refusal (the access-control check — most notable gap), StoreWriteFailed/FailedStateWriteFailed (the write-failure → FailedManualIntervention fallback and both-failed), and RecoveryRefused (stale evidence / still-breaching daily PnL). The store-level fail-closed reasons are well covered, but the command's mapping of corrupt/oversized/version → StoreFailClosed is not exercised. Adding an unauthorized-operator test in particular would lock down the one check that gates who can re-arm live trading.

5. NOTE (not a defect) — Effective recovery gate is narrower than "drives evaluate_losdrawdown_breaches(0,0,limit)=false (confirmed at loss_governor.rs:304-310), the per-trade and drawdown dimensions always pass — so evaluate_loss_admission only genuinely re-checks daily/rolling PnL. The real gate is: authorized operator + valid/fresh evidence + persisted daily PnL within limits. Also, evidence_sha256 is format-validated only (strict 64-char lowercase hex) and is never verified against an actual file — it's operator-attested audit metadata, not a cryptographic gate; the command never opens evidence_path. This mirrors the runtime path (so it's consistent, not a regression), and the zeroed dimensions are backstopped by the live loss-governor re-evaluating fresh account state on node restart. Worth stating plainly so no one over-trusts "re-evaluArmed+snapshot+audit / write-failure handling — Holds. Only Halting|Halted with trigger.kind == LossGovernorBreach reach a write (loss_governor_recoverable_trading_state); everything else → UnsupportedState/NonLossGovernorState. Success writes Armed + carried loss_protection + appended audit; recovery-write failure writes FailedManualIntervention, both-failed is a distinct loud FailedStateWriteFailed. The unreachable! in failed_manual_intervention_state is genuinely unreachable (guarded by the prior loss_governor_recoverable_trading_state gate). Minor design note: a Halting (actions in-flight) recovers straight to Armed, bypassing halt-action completion — inherent to operator override.
2. Evidence contract + authorized-operator — Holds. No path bypasses LossGovernorManualRecoveryEvidence::new (operator_id non-empty, strict sha256, observed_at≠0, path non-empty/relative/no-..); re-validated inside the state machine (defense in depth). authorized_operator_ids comes from risk.kill_switch; empty ⇒ always refuse (fail-closed); exact-string match, no trim/case bypass. (Coverage gap #4.)
3. Fail-closed store handling — Holds. Missing→MissingStore (no bootstrap, tested), corrupt/oversized/wrong-version→StoreFailClosed, non-loss→NonLossGovernorState, unsupported→UnsupportedState; no auto-create; each distinct and loud.
4. Schema compat both directions — Holds. Schema stays 2 (unbumped — no hunk touches the const). Old store→new binary: serde defaults missing Option to None→empty history — proven transitively by the green happy-path test (writes empty-history store = absent field, then re-loads and recovers). New store→old binary: base struct has no deny_unknown_fields, so the additive field is ignored and state is read correctly — not a silent misread; only audit metadata is invisible on rollback.
5. Audit-history preservation + log on failed read — Holds on the happy path and the Err(Io) branch (the regression test genuinely forces EACCES → Err, asserts the drop and the loud log). Gap per finding #2 on the corrupt/oversized Ok(FailClosed) reads. Other writers are safe: write_loss_governor_manual_recovery uses the passed record (no re-read); bootstrap is O_EXCL (can't overwrite).

Suggested disposition: address #1 (or explicitly accept it with an alarm) and #2 before this is exercised at scale; #3/#4 are cheap hardening; #5 is context operators need. None block the core guarantees. Want me to file these as one consolidated follow-up issue (MECE, numbered sub-bullets per my usual pattern) or hand a fix brief to Codex for #1/#2?

   2. Evidence contract — holds.
      Every path constructs LossGovernorManualRecoveryEvidence
       via ::new, which validates operator id, SHA-256,
      observed-at, and path limits

   3. Fail-closed store handling — holds for the listed cases.
      Missing → MissingEvidence → MissingStore; corrupt →
      CorruptEvidence; oversized → OversizedEvidence; wrong
      schema → UnsupportedSchemaVersion; non-loss-governor
      trigger → NonLossGovernorState; unsupported state kinds
      → UnsupportedState. No auto-create; history is
      append-only. The error messages are loud and include the
      path.

   4. Schema compatibility — forward OK, backward unsafe.
      Old store + new binary: loss_governor_manual_recoveries
      is Option<...> and defaults to empty
      (src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs:266-272).
      New store + old binary: the old PersistedKillSwitchState
       has no #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)], so the old binary
      silently ignores the new field, reads
      state/loss_protection normally, and on its next write
      re-serializes without the audit history. This is silent
      misread/data loss, not fail-closed.

   5. Audit-history preservation — holds for intended paths,

      write_state_with_loss_snapshot re-reads and carries
      history forward

      bootstrap_initial_armed_loss_snapshot correctly starts

T1a Node: existing_loss_governor_manual_recoveries() reads store → gets OLD history (N records)
T2  Recovery: write_loss_governor_manual_recovery atomic-renames → store now has N+1 records
T1b Node: serialize(state, snapshot, OLD N records) → atomic rename → overwrites T2
Result: the recovery's audit record is silently lost. The node carried forward the pre-recovery history. The node's subsequent state write is fail-safe for trading state (it re-evaluates and may re-halt), but the audit trail has a gap.
The window is the entire write_state_with_loss_snapshot call (read → serialize → rename). There is no file lock, PID check, or advisory mutex.

- **Option B: evidence-gated override** — the whole point of *manual* recovery is operator judgment, so valid evidence + authorized operator clears the halt regardless of the stored snapshot. More useful, more dangerous, and it changes what the #1185-era state machine means.

Here's the situation in plain English:

**What we built:** a command that lets a human un-freeze the bot after it halted itself for losing too much money. Until now, no such command existed — if the bot froze, there was no official way to un-freeze it.

**What the reviewers found — two things:**

1. **A storage mistake (being fixed, no decision needed).** The command writes a permanent logbook entry every time someone un-freezes the bot — but it stores that logbook *inside* the same small safety file the bot uses to remember whether it's frozen. That file has a strict size cap. Enough entries and the file fills up, and in the worst chain of events the bot's emergency cleanup *wipes the whole logbook*. The fix is obvious and already in the work order: keep the logbook in its own separate file.

2. **A question only you can answer.** Before un-freezing, the command re-checks the loss numbers saved at the moment of the freeze. But those saved numbers *are the numbers that caused the freeze* — they still say "too much loss." So as written, the command refuses to clear the very freeze it was built to clear. There are two ways to define what this command should be:

- **Option A — the check wins (my recommendation).** A human cannot un-freeze the bot while the saved numbers still say the loss limit is breached. The command only clears freezes whose cause has genuinely passed (say, a new trading day). If you want to trade again despite the loss, you change the loss limit through a proper config change — with review — not through this command. Safety-first, consistent with everything else we've built.
- **Option B — the human wins.** An authorized operator with a signed-off evidence file can force the un-freeze regardless of the numbers. More convenient in a crisis, but it means one person's judgment can outrank the loss limit — which is exactly what the kill-switch exists to prevent.

Say "A" or "B" and the work order goes out.
I still did not understand

Simpler version:

The bot has an automatic emergency brake: lose too much money, and it stops itself. We just built the key that releases that brake — it didn't exist before.

The question is: **should the key work while the "too much loss" warning light is still on?**

- **Option A:** No. The key only works once the warning has cleared (for example, a new trading day has started). If the light is still on and you want to trade anyway, you have to formally raise the loss limit in the settings — a deliberate, reviewed change. *The machine has the final word.*
- **Option B:** Yes. If you're an authorized person, turning the key releases the brake even while the light is still on. *The human has the final word.*

I recommend **A** — the whole reason the brake exists is to stop trading during a losing streak, and a brake anyone can bypass in the moment isn't much of a brake.

That's the entire decision: A or B?
A

Honest answer: the rounds are converging (each round's findings are smaller — correctness → coverage → shape-completeness → doc accuracy), so the process is working. But you're right that there's a pattern underneath, and it's not a *new* class — it's the two classes your tech-debt audit already named, and my fix briefs have been paying interest on them instead of principal:

**1. No single source of truth in the data itself.** #1222 needed four rounds because "a committed hash-pin" turns out to exist in *three different ad-hoc shapes* in the reference tree — because nothing ever defined ONE canonical way to record provenance. Each generator invented its own. So the gate we built had to *discover* the shapes empirically, one panel round at a time. The gate is a compensating control for a missing schema. Same story with the trailing newlines: some files hand-touched, some generator-written, no enforced format.

**2. Dual implementations.** #1218 needed four rounds because the maker's bounds exist as *two hand-written copies* (live validator + config validator), so we built a parity test — and then spent two rounds discovering the parity test's own blind spots. A parity test between two copies is scaffolding; the terminal fix (one shared bounds function, already on the cleanup ledger) makes the whole test unnecessary.

**And one process lesson that's mine:** my fix briefs said "cover the listed items" — Codex covered the list, and the next panel found the list was incomplete. Checklists invite this. The briefs should demand *completeness proofs* — "derive the full set from the code/data and show the derivation" — which is exactly what finally happened in #1222 round 3 when a reviewer counted every pin repo-wide instead of checking the named ones.

What I'd change going forward:

- **Cap the enumeration.** #1222 stops after round 4 regardless; the durable fix goes on the ledger as its own item: one canonical pin schema, emitted by every generator, with the gate validating schema conformance instead of guessing shapes. That work naturally belongs with the sweep-runner era (Briefs 5–6) which touches this tree anyway.
- **#1218's terminal fix stays tracked:** extract the shared bounds function; the parity test then shrinks from safety net to smoke check.
- **Brief format change:** every gate-style fix must state the closed-form definition of what it covers and prove the enumeration, not enumerate examples.

So: not a missing class — the *known* diseases (no-SSOT, dual-path) showing up in the backtester's data layer, plus a brief-writing habit of mine that let them cost one extra round each. Both now have named fixes.
dual implementation cannot exist.

Understood — and applying that rule honestly means admitting my round-2 brief *created* this one. The maker's validator originally had a deliberate "one home per concern" design (bounds lived only in the archetype — the old doc comment said exactly that). When the panel found the validation gap, my fix brief said "bring validate_config to parity by *mirroring* the live bounds" — which manufactured a hand-copy, i.e., a dual implementation, and then a parity test to police the copy. That's the gate-as-fix pattern your standing rule already bans. The correct fix was always: **one shared bounds implementation, called by both** — the precedent even exists in the same file (the portfolio bounds already work that way via the shared blocker function).

I didn't understand - explain very concisely

Very simply:

**All these findings are one problem wearing different costumes.**

The backtester keeps a folder of record files — like a filing cabinet of receipts. The problem: **there was never one official way to write those files.** Different tools wrote them in slightly different formats, and receipts reference each other by fingerprint with no standard for how fingerprints are recorded.

So every review round digs up another symptom of that same missing standard:

- Round 1: a test was overwriting a filed receipt.
- Round 2: fixing one receipt broke its fingerprint in another file.
- Rounds 3–4: fingerprints turn out to be recorded in *three different styles*, and the checker only knew one.
- Round 5 (today): the tool that fixed 7,890 fingerprints rewrote the files in *yet another format* — committing the same sin it was fixing.

**Why it repeats:** we've been building a better and better *checker*. But a checker can only catch mess; it can't prevent it. The real fix is a rule like the one you gave for code — "two ways of writing the same thing cannot exist" — applied to these files: one official format, one official writing tool, everything else forbidden.

**Plan:** round 5 is the last cleanup round on this PR. After that, the "one official writer" fix becomes its own work item, and any leftover mess gets caught by the checker automatically — not by more review rounds.
so when do we do the one official writer fix

As soon as #1222 merges — it becomes the very next backtester-lane brief (call it **Brief 9**), and here's the ordering logic:

1. **It must wait for #1222** only because it edits the same files and tests — running them concurrently guarantees conflicts.
2. **It must come *before* Brief 6 (the sweep-runner)**, because the sweep-runner is the next thing that *writes new record files* — building it before the official-writer rule exists would mint new files in yet another format. Born-canonical beats cleaned-up-later.
3. **Brief 5 (the real-history test into CI) doesn't touch the record folder at all**, so it runs in parallel with Brief 9 — no ordering constraint.

So the queue after #1222 lands: **#1219 resumes + Brief 5 and Brief 9 in parallel → then Brief 6.**

What Brief 9 will contain (I'll draft it the day #1222 merges, anchored at whatever main looks like then): one sanctioned writing function for the reference tree that every generator and tool must call (raw UTF-8, no trailing newline, one pin shape — the format the checker already expects); a one-time pass re-writing existing files through it with all fingerprints updated in lockstep (the gate #1222 built holds that honest); and a test that fails if any code path writes to the reference tree without going through the sanctioned writer — so a second writer can't quietly come back.
and why are we not doing that now

Three concrete reasons, in order of weight:

1. **The safety net for that fix *is* #1222.** Rewriting every record file through the official writer is exactly the kind of mass change that goes wrong silently — round 4 just proved it (a "simple" fingerprint fix quietly re-encoded two whole files). The fingerprint checker #1222 is finishing is what makes the big rewrite safe: any pin the rewrite forgets or breaks turns CI red instead of shipping. Doing the rewrite *before* the checker merges means doing it without the net — the exact mistake we'd be trying to cure.

2. **Same files, guaranteed collision.** Brief 9 rewrites the very JSON files and touches the very test #1222's round 5 is editing right now. Two sessions editing 10,000-line JSON files in parallel ends in merge conflicts that are themselves a source of silent data errors.

3. **The wait is hours, not weeks.** #1222 is one small, well-defined round from done, and your Codex sessions are already saturated with three active rounds. Starting a fourth heavy brief now buys almost no calendar time and adds real risk.

If #1222 stalls for some reason, the fallback is to split Brief 9 and start only its code half (the writer function and the no-bypass test, which don't touch #1222's files) — but on the current pace that optimization isn't worth the coordination overhead.

A. LOW — audit append has no torn-line defense; one partial line makes the whole trail unloadable

src/bolt_v3_atomic_io.rs append_private_file + src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs load_loss_governor_manual_recoveries.

Append is O_APPEND + sync_all, so a clean crash keeps lines whole. But under power-loss mid-write, a torn line (no trailing \n) can persist;recovery or the command (which counts, not parses), so it's contained — but the audit history becomes unreadable via load_... and the line-count undercounts. Cheap fix: tolerate/skip a single unparseable trailing line on load, or write a leading \n defensively. This directly answers the brief's "partial line on crash?" question.

B. LOW — line-count reads the whole sidecar into memory per append; unbounded growth undocumented

src/bolt_v3_kill_switch_store.rs loss_governor_manual_recovery_audit_line_count.

fs::read_to_string loads the entire file on every append (O(n)/append, O(n²) cumulative; OOM risk if the sidecar ever grows large). Growth is now decoupled from the safety file (good — that was round-1 #1), but it's plain unbounded disk with no stated rotation/retention policy. Rare-event log, so low practical impact; worth a one-line "unbounded, rotate externally" note and an O(1) count (seek-to-end or byte-scan) if you care.

With any loss_governor config that sets max_per_trade_loss/max_rolling_loss/max_drawdown (the test fixture sets all three), the command always refuses via MissingDimensionFailClosed — those dimensions have no durable snapshot data.       it.

This panel round settled the redesign — **all four reviewers confirmed round-1's findings are structurally dissolved** (two of them proved the differential claims by construction, closing the missing-red-proof caveat). But it also surfaced a structural truth about Option A that needs one more decision from you.

**The discovery (all four reviewers, from different angles):** under any *real* production config, this command **can never succeed**. Config validation requires all four loss limits to be set; the durable store only records the daily loss; so three of the four checks always hit "no data → refuse." The success-path tests only pass because they hand-build a config that validation would reject. Worse, it's not just missing data — it's physics: an offline command inspects a *frozen* snapshot from the moment of the halt, and frozen breach numbers never un-breach, they just go stale (which also refuses). **Strict Option A plus "node stopped" equals a command that always says no.**

That's not what you decided — you chose "the machine has the final word," not "the answer is always no." Two ways to honor your rule and still have a working command:

- **A1 — keep it strict.** The offline command stays as-is (a refusal machine with good diagnostics); real recovery happens later via the *running* node (where fresh data exists for every check) once we build an operator channel to the runtime recovery function. More design work, deferred usefulness.
- **A2 (my recommendation) — let the calendar count as machine evidence.** Some conditions provably pass by *time alone*: a daily-loss halt is over when the UTC day has rolled; a rolling-window halt is over when the window has elapsed since the halt. Those are clock facts the machine can verify offline — no human judgment, no override. Halts based on drawdown/per-trade (unverifiable offline) still refuse and wait for the runtime path. This makes the command work for the by-far-most-common case (yesterday's daily-loss halt) while keeping your rule fully intact.

**The rest of the panel's findings are small and consensus** — queued for round 3 regardless of your choice: tolerate a torn final line in the audit file (crash mid-write currently makes the whole trail unreadable); validate on append so a corrupt audit file can't silently accept new lines; **also audit *refused* attempts** (currently only successes are recorded — incident reviewers can't see that someone tried and was denied); fix one misleading diagnostic (stale evidence reports as the wrong reason); document the file's unbounded-growth/rotation expectation; one integration test.

Say **A1** or **A2** and I'll cut the round-3 brief.

explain the situation in plain english and make this very concise

The un-freeze command we built has a logic trap:

**To un-freeze, the machine re-checks "is the danger over?" But a stopped bot has no fresh data — only the numbers frozen at the moment it froze. Those numbers always still say "danger." So the command, as built, always answers no. It's a key that never turns.**

Two ways out, both keeping your rule that the machine decides:

- **A1:** Leave it strict. The key stays useless for now; later we build a way to ask the *running* bot (which has fresh data) to un-freeze itself.
- **A2 (recommended):** Let the machine accept **clock facts**. "The trading day that caused the loss has ended" is something the machine can verify from the calendar alone — no human judgment. So yesterday's daily-loss freeze becomes clearable today; freeze types that can't be verified by clock alone still refuse.

Everything else from the review is minor housekeeping and proceeds either way.

**A1 or A2?**

so is it difficult to add new strategies like this? do we need to keep doing a lot of code work to add more strategies?

Honest answer: **today it's still too much code work, and it's the exact same disease you banned for venues.**

What adding the maker to the backtester actually required (beyond the review rounds, which were mostly paying down pre-existing debt): the strategy logic itself lives in one module — that part is legitimate, unavoidable work — but wiring it in meant editing about **five separate shared-code sites**: the registry key list, the parameters list, a validation arm, a build arm, plus tests. That's "strategy N+1 = shared-code surgery," which is precisely what your venue deal-breaker forbids for venues.

The root cause is already named in your architecture map: the strategy roster is **triple-booked** — the live registry, the backtester's allowlist, and the parameter lists each independently know which strategies exist. Three copies of one fact. Under your no-dual-implementation rule, that's not allowed to survive.

The target state (and it's step ⑤ in the already-mapped build order): **one strategy descriptor** — a single registry entry that carries the key, config schema, validation, and build function — with both the live node and the backtester *deriving* everything from it. Then adding a strategy = write the strategy module + add one registry row. Zero shared-code edits. Same acceptance test as venues: if strategy N+1 touches anything beyond its own module and one registry line, the PR is rejected.

Two things worth knowing:

1. **The marginal cost already dropped a lot.** #1218's five rounds consolidated the validation into one home and built shared registration helpers — the *next* strategy arm would be maybe a third of the work. But a third of "too much" still fails your standard.
2. **The remaining gap has a natural vehicle:** the registration-robustness cleanup brief already queued (taker-helper migration, panic class, error taxonomy) is the same files — I'll fold the roster-to-one-descriptor consolidation into its design so the whole thing lands as one coherent "strategies become registry rows" change rather than another incremental round.

So: current answer — still real code work per strategy; committed direction — one module plus one row, enforced by the same deal-breaker rule as venues.
okay - so what I did not understand is the strategy itself lives in the code already - I don't know what we are doing if we can just play that strategy that lives somewhere in our code

Right — the strategy's brain already existed in the code. What was missing is best explained with an analogy:

**The strategy is a race car that already sits in the garage. The backtester is a racing simulator — a video game. The car existing in the garage doesn't mean the game knows how to load it.**

Three things had to happen, and only the first was ever supposed to be work:

1. **The simulator kept a hard list of which cars it would load** — three names, and the maker wasn't one of them. Ask for it and the simulator refused outright. Adding the name to the list was genuinely small.
2. **Loading a car into the simulator needs hookup plumbing** — in the simulation, the strategy's inputs are fake (replayed historical prices, simulated fees, simulated order fills), so someone has to connect the real brain to the fake world. The good news from #1218: it connects through the *same* construction machinery the live system uses — so the simulated maker is literally the live maker, not a copy.
3. **The five review rounds were mostly not about any of that** — they were pre-existing debt the work exposed: the strategy's config checking existed in two hand-written copies, the "did it load?" test proved nothing, etc. That was cleanup we'd have paid eventually, and it's why the next strategy costs a fraction of this one.

Your instinct is exactly the end state we've now committed to: since the live system already has a registry that knows how to build every strategy, the simulator should just *read that registry* — no list of its own, no per-strategy plumbing. Then "play a strategy that lives in our code" becomes what you expect: one registry row, and both the live system and the simulator can run it.

The bin/*.rs references are println! debugging only. ✓
Break-2: Data neutrality — PASS
Zero committed reference bytes changed in round 6 (empty diffstat for specs/023-.../reference/). The two retained runs/00000 records (1 binance + 1 bybit) were already file-byte hashes from round-5 reconciliation. The new code computes sha256_hex(&bytes) where bytes = serde_json::to_vec_pretty(plan) — the exact bytes passed to atomic_write. Since the committed plan files ARE pretty-written, sha256_hex(&pretty_bytes) == sha256(committed_file_bytes), so the fixed generator agrees with the round-5 pins. so what deos tier 1 do? I didn't fully understand

Tier 1's job in one sentence: **stop the kinds of damage you can't undo, before doing anything ambitious.**

There are three kinds of "can't undo" it targets, and here's what each finished piece actually does for you:

**1. Losing evidence forever.**
- *Brief 1 (merged):* when the bot exits a trade, it now permanently records the prices it saw. Before, it calculated them and threw them away — so bad exits couldn't be investigated after the fact.
- *Brief 8 (finishing):* the backtester's filing cabinet of record files was quietly corruptible — a test was overwriting filed records, and fingerprints could silently rot. Now every fingerprint is checked on every CI run, and the tools can't write mismatched records anymore.
- *Still to come in Tier 1:* the data recorder — market data that's gone forever if nobody saves it live.

**2. Breaking live trading through avoidable accidents.**
- *Brief 2 (merged):* a settings file that no longer matched the code would previously sail through all checks and only explode when the bot tried to boot on the real machine. Now that mismatch fails CI the moment it's created.
- *Brief 3 (in progress):* if the bot halts itself for losing too much, there was literally no command to un-halt it — a human would have to hand-edit files on the server. Now there's a proper command, with your two rules baked in: the machine decides, and the calendar counts as proof.

**3. Nobody-owns-it problems.** Seven known weaknesses (like the live-approval check running on placeholder zeros) had no owner and no ticket — invisible work rots. Filing the two ownership issues (still owed by me) makes them impossible to lose.

**Why it comes first:** everything after Tier 1 — backtesting campaigns, live micro-trades, the edge verdict — *generates* evidence and *runs* live sessions. Doing that on top of a system that silently loses records and can strand itself mid-halt means every later result is untrustworthy and every live test carries dumb risk. Tier 1 is making the ground solid before building on it.

Yes — my lane is backtesting, research analytics, dashboard, and the data layer under them. Here's the roadmap, and then the honest answer on hardcoding.

**The roadmap (five phases, each feeding the next):**

1. **Now — solid ground (Tier 1 tail).** Finish the in-flight PRs: record-keeping that can't silently rot, config that can't silently drift, a halt that can be recovered. Done this week.
2. **Data substrate.** One official writer for all record files (Brief 9); the certified real-history P/L test becomes a required CI gate (Brief 5); strategies become registry rows instead of code surgery (registration-robustness brief); and the continuous market-data recorder gets designed — the venue-agnostic framework that records perishable data whether or not we're trading.
3. **Research analytics on one spine.** The sweep-runner front door (Brief 6) turns the backtester from "runs one test when asked" into "produces a growing, queryable corpus of results with one index." Analytics reads that corpus — one data spine, no parallel pipelines.
4. **Dashboard.** The decision viewer (buildable today), then trades/positions/P&L views, then the calibration scoreboard — which needs the campaign's settlement recorder (#36) to exist, because a scoreboard without real outcomes is fiction.
5. **The verdict loop.** Backtest corpus + live micro-trade evidence flow into calibration → "is the edge real?" gets answered with data → scaling decisions (more venues, more strategies) become registry-row changes, not projects.

**On hardcoding — the honest status:** the *infrastructure* in all five phases carries no venue, no asset class, no market assumptions: the backtest engine is NautilusTrader's (it runs equities, FX, futures, options, crypto identically), catalogs and record formats are instrument-agnostic, the venue comes from the manifest/registry, and strategies load through the production registry. Named things are allowed to exist in exactly **two sanctioned places**: per-venue data adapters (something must speak each venue's protocol — isolated, one module each) and strategy modules themselves (a strategy may legitimately *be about* binary options — that's its content, not the platform's). Everything outside those two places that still carries venue vocabulary is known, enumerated debt on a mandated cleanup list — the 17 hardcoded venue reject-strings in the taker (your required cleanup, unblocked by yesterday's Lane 4 merge) and some `polymarket_*`-named fields in shared records. Those get removed, not grandfathered.

So the end state you should hold me to: a backtesting/analytics/dashboard platform where running a new strategy on a new venue in a new asset class changes registry rows and adds an adapter — and the pipeline, the corpus, the scoreboard, and the dashboards don't know the difference.
so I don't understand why we have so much work - tier 1 has 9 briefs and research analytics + backtesting engine itself took a lot of work even before starting this with you

Fair frustration. The honest answer has three parts:

**1. Most of this work wasn't created — it was uncovered.** Tier 1 was scoped as four small fixes. It became nine briefs because nearly every "small fix" hit pre-existing, invisible defects: Brief 4 tripped over a test that had been corrupting committed files *for weeks* (hidden by CI luck), which became Brief 8, which uncovered unchecked fingerprints, which uncovered a generator that's been recording wrong hashes since it was written. None of that was new damage. It was already in the codebase you paid for — silent, waiting to surface during something worse, like a live incident. Your own records say why: hundreds of issues were closed before with sessions optimizing for "done," and the result was work that *looked* correct while quietly compounding. This week is that bill being paid down — visibly, this time.

**2. Some of the volume is your quality bar, deliberately.** Panel rounds, red proofs, class-fixes-not-patches — a cheaper process would have finished #1222 in two rounds instead of seven. It also would have shipped the re-encoded data files, the forked validator, and the hash-minting generator, and you'd be paying for those in six months at 10x. You chose "80% done is 0% done"; this is what that costs up front and what it saves later.

**3. The reason to believe it converges — it already is.** Watch the marginal costs: adding the maker to the backtester took five rounds; the next strategy takes a fraction, and after the registry-row work, near zero. The fingerprint class can't recur. The hash-drift class can't recur. The fixture-mutation class can't recur. Every one of these was killed *structurally* — a gate or a single-implementation rule makes the mistake impossible, not just detected. Debt retired this way stays retired, which is exactly what didn't happen in the previous 800 issues.

The uncomfortable summary: the earlier BTE/RA effort built real machinery *and* a large hidden defect inventory, because nothing checked. That inventory is finite, we've been burning through its biggest classes all week, and the curve you should expect — and hold me to — is each next brief costing less than the last.

The rest of the panel consolidates into small, consensus polish — round-4 brief (final):

```
PR #1226 round 4 — final polish from the panel. Same branch/worktree. No merge.
NOTE for the PR body: one panel HIGH ("production halts never populate loss_halt_reason") was
DISPROVEN by direct read — halt_for_realized_loss_breach calls loss_governor_breach_with_reason
at loss_protection.rs:437. Record that with the anchor; no action.

FIX 1 (audit truth, GPT Medium): the pre-state-write audit line currently says
outcome="recovered" before the Armed write succeeds — a crash in between leaves a durable
"recovered" record for a still-halted store. Relabel the pre-write line outcome="attempted";
append outcome="recovered" ONLY after the state write succeeds; write-failed path unchanged.
Document: the LAST record per attempt is authoritative.

FIX 2 (proportional remediation, Claude): a torn final audit line currently escalates the NEXT
recovery attempt into writing FailedManualIntervention — converting a bookkeeping blemish into
a terminal halt state. TornManualRecoveryAudit must instead return a distinct
"repair-the-audit-file-and-retry" error that leaves the halt state UNTOUCHED.

FIX 3 (audit completeness, GPT/GLM): audit every refusal reachable after config load —
add NonLossGovernorState, UnsupportedState, invalid-evidence, missing-snapshot, and
store-fail-closed refusals to the audited set (an authorized-or-not human ran the command;
forensics should see it). Document the non-auditable boundary (pre-config failures, unwritable
audit path) in the module doc.

FIX 4 (docs, GPT/Kimi): state explicitly that the ROLLING window authority is the CURRENT
config value (a config change is the sanctioned lever, visible in review; the live re-check at
node start is the backstop) — and align the wording to the strict boundary ("more than the
full window must have elapsed"; exact-equality refuses).

FIX 5 (DRY, Kimi): NANOS_PER_UTC_DAY is defined in two files — move it to the shared numeric
home, both call sites import it.

FIX 6 (test fidelity, GLM): the test helper persists halts by patching JSON strings; use the
typed loss_governor_breach_with_reason constructor so tests exercise the production
serialization path.

EVIDENCE (standard): verify-remote full dispatch at FINAL head; if the Rust Probe infra
cooperates, one red quote for FIX 1 (attempted-vs-recovered) — otherwise declare the deviation
as before; body updated; FINAL REPORT.
